QF.id: AIFM CII Fund Performance and Benchmarking_10

question.text: For Category I and II AIFs, benchmarking agencies typically construct 'vintage-year' benchmarks. What is a 'vintage year' in this context?

answer.text: The calendar year in which the fund files its final winding-up return with SEBI.
The year in which the benchmarking agency's data vendor was incorporated.
The year in which the fund achieves its First Close — used to group funds with comparable investment-deployment timelines.
The year in which the LP first recovers 100% of paid-in capital (DPI = 1.0).

explanation.text: The Logic: Per Chapter 7 footnote 60 and Section 7.6, vintage year refers to the milestone year in which the first influx of investment capital is deployed — in AIF context, typically anchored to First Close. Vintage grouping ensures apples-to-apples comparison because funds of the same vintage face the same macro entry pricing and exit conditions. The Trap: A is the wind-up, not vintage. C is nonsensical. D is called the 'DPI breakeven year', a separate performance milestone. Cross-Exam Context: XIX-C tests the same definition. XIX-A uses vintage for LP allocation pitch. Cambridge Associates, Preqin and PitchBook globally publish vintage-year quartiles — the Cat I/II Manager must know where their fund sits. Manager's Pro-Tip: When fundraising, NEVER show absolute IRR without stating your vintage and quartile. 'Top-quartile of 2019 India Growth vintage' is a defensible claim; raw '22% IRR' without vintage context invites LP scepticism.
